### 7.99

*ekākṣara-pādo yathā,*

**Перевод:**

**Each line has only one type of consonant:**

*śaṁ-śīḥ śaśī śaśāśāśāṁ*  
*pāpo ’papāpa-paḥ papiḥ*  
*lolo lalāla līlā-līṁ*  
*yayāyaṁ yo ’yayā yayau*

**Пословный перевод:**

sam—\[my\] happiness; sih—\[the moon,\] which is apathetic toward (or which destroys); sasi—the moon; sasasa—jumped; asam—to \[another\] direction (or desire); papah—wicked; apa-papa—sinless people (i.e. us gopis) (“from whom sin is gone (apa = apagata)”); pah—withers (from the verbal root pai sosane (to dry)); papih— the moon (“it drinks”); lolah—Krsna (“He thirsts \[for gopis\]”); lalala—desired; lila—during pastimes; lim—a girl who embraces (from the verbal root li\[n\] slesane) (or lila-alim— \[Krsna desired\] a series of pastimes); yaya—with which girl \[who embraces during pastimes\]; ayam—good fortune (i.e. union); yah—who (Krsna); ayaya—with her who was not going (i.e. who was fixed on union and was not displaying any contrariness); yayau—attained.

**Перевод:**

**\[While going to meet Krsna, a certain gopi suddenly sees the newly risen moon. Unable to meet Him, she laments:\]**

**The moon is not awake to my happiness. It has suddenly shifted to another direction. The wicked moon withers sinless girls like us and frustrates our desires. Krsna thirsts for gopis. He wanted a girl who will embrace Him during foreplay. He must be having union with such a girl by now, and surely that girl will not leave Him.**

**Комментарий:**

Visvanatha Cakravarti: *śaṁ-śīḥ śaṁ kalyāṇaṁ tatra śete na tu mat-kalyāṇe jāgartīty arthaḥ, śīṅ svapne kvib-antaḥ, yadvā matkalyāṇasya śīr hiṁsā yataḥ, śṝ hiṁsāyāṁ sampad-ādi-kvip, śam iti māntam avyayam,* “Sam is an indeclinable word meaning kalyana (auspiciousness, happiness); sam-sih is a krt-samasa (a verbal compound) made from the verbal root si\[n\] svapne (to rest, sleep) and the suffix kvip in the actice voice: “\[The moon\] is not awake to my happiness.” Alternatively, sam-sih is a bahuvrihi compound, “that because of which there is the end of my well-being,” where sih is originally a feminine word which means himsa (harm, destruction), made from the verbal root sr himsayam and the suffix kvip.”

na—the man (the Purusa); nana—many; na—not; an-inah—He has no master (or He other than whom there is no master); anenah— is sinless; nana—various; anena—by Him; ananam—the life; nu— obviously; nuh—of a living entity; nunam—indeed; na—not; unan—tiny (i.e. humans); nrn—persons; anunan—not tiny (i.e. demigods); anu—directed toward; na—not; nut—praise; nut—one who dispels; nu—certainly; unninih—constantly leads upwards.

**Перевод:**

**The Supreme Person is not manifold. Obviously, He has no master and is sinless. Indeed, He created this variegated universe and is the life of every living being. Certainly, He never prevents praise directed at exalted individuals nor even at insignificant people. Is He not a constant uplifter?**

**Комментарий:**

Visvanatha Cakravarti: “The Lord thinks, “Let anyone praise a demigod as the Lord, whether that demigod is minute or elevated.” In that way the Lord has no intolerance. He constantly leads one upward (unninih = urdhvam nitaram nayati iti sah), to Svarga, Maharloka, and so forth. The idea is: Only He makes a person, even a worshiper of a god, whether the god is minute or elevated, obtain the result, such as Svarga, since only He is the giver of all results” (Subodhim).

Visvanatha Cakaravarti says the adjective anenah (sinless) is like the statement: ayam atmapahata-papma, “He, the Soul, is sinless” (Chandogya Upanisad 8.1.5). As an alternative explanation, he glosses anenah as niraparadhah (He did no wrong) in the sense that He is not at fault for creating a world where there is disparity (Subodhini).

### 7.101

*siṁhāvaloka-ślokāntara-garbho yathā,*

**Перевод:**

**This verse contains another verse, by the axiom called “a lion’s glance” (taking a look back). \[The verse it contains is shown afterwards.\]**

*tejaḥ kiñcana tat tad asya satataṁ navyāmbudābhaṁ bhaja*  
*snigdhaṁ locana-lobha-daṁ caturatā-līlā-vilāsāvali*  
*antaś-cintayatāṁ rasasya saraṇiṁ śrī-rādhikā-prauḍhima-*  
*premārdraṁ rucira-cchavi smaravatīṁ krīḍāṁ dadhad dhāmasu*

**Пословный перевод:**

tejah—the effulgence; kincana—indescribable; tat—well-known; tat—that; asya—His; satatam—always; navya—new; ambuda—of a cloud; abham—which has the sheen; bhaja—you should worship; snigdham—lovely (or lovingly); locana—to the eyes; lobha-dam — gives greed; caturata—endowed with expertise; lila-vilasa—of playful pastimes; avali—because of which \[effulgence\] there is a multitude; antah-cintayatam—for people (“who are thinking internally (with their hearts)”); rasasya—of rasa; saranim—is the path; sri-radhika—of Sri Radhika; praudhima—on account of the boldness; prema—with love; ardram—it melts; rucira—is attractive; chavi—its luster; smaravafim—which contain Cupid; kridam—pastimes; dadhat—is nourishing; dhamasu—in places.

**Перевод:**

**Always lovingly worship Krsna’s effulgence. It gives rise to playful and clever pastimes. It resembles the sheen of a new raincloud and makes the eyes greedy. It is the path of rasa for those who think with their hearts. Its attractive luster overflows with love on account of Sri Radhika’s boldness and enhances the love games in the pleasure groves.**

### 7.102

*atra,*

**Перевод:**

**This verse is contained in the previous one. (In each line, the first series of syllables is at the end of the same line in the above verse, and the rest of the syllables are from the same line.)**

*navyāmbudābhaṁ bhaja tat tad asya*  
*līlā-vilāsāvali-lobha-daṁ ca*  
*śrī-rādhikā-prauḍhi-matāṁ rasasya*  
*krīḍāṁ dadhad dhāma sura-cchavi sma*

*iti ślokāntara-garbhaḥ*

**Пословный перевод:**

navya—new; ambuda—of a cloud; abham—that which has the splendor; bhaja—worship; tat—that; tat—well-known; asya— His; lila-vilasa—of playful pastimes; avali—for a multitude; lobha-dam—which creates greed; ca—and; sri-radhika—of Sri Radhika; praudhi—because of the boldness; matam—which are celebrated; rasasya—of rasa; kridam—pastimes; dadhat—which is nourishing; dhama—the effulgence; sura—of the gods; chavi— because of which \[effulgence\] there is the splendor; sma—was (sma = bhavati sma).

**Перевод:**

**Revere Krsna’s effulgence. The sun god and other gods shine because of it. It is the source of the brahmajyoti. It resembles the sheen of a new raincloud. By seeing Krsna’s splendor, one longs to participate in His delightful pastimes. His beauty sustains the games of rasa, celebrated because of Sri Radhika’s display of self-assertion.**

**Комментарий:**

Visvanatha Cakravarti glosses dhama as tejah (effulgence). The definition is: grha-deha-tvit-prabhava dhamani, “Dhama means house, body, effulgence, and power” (Amara-kosa 3.3.124).

Visvanatha Cakravarti expounds: The compound sura-cchavi means: suranam suryadinam api chavis tejo yasmat, “\[The effulgence,\] because of which there is the gods’ effulgence,” and is used in reference to these three texts:

*na tad bhāsayate sūryo na śaśāṅko na pāvakaḥ*  
*yad gatvā na nivartante tad dhāma paramaṁ mama*

**“That topmost abode of Mine is not illumined by the sun, nor by the moon, nor by fire. Those who go there never return” (Bhagavad­gita 15.6).**

*yad āditya-gataṁ tejo jagad bhāsayate ’khilam*  
*yac candramasi yac cāgnau tat tejo viddhi māmakam*

**“You should know that the sun’s effulgence, which illuminates the whole world, the splendor of the moon and the radiance of fire are My manifestations of might” (Bhagavad-gita** [**15.12**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/bg/15.12)**).**

*na tatra sūryo bhāti na candra-tārakaṁ*  
*nemā vidyuto bhānti kuto ’yam agniḥ*  
*tam eva bhāntam anu bhāti sarvaṁ*  
*tasya bhāsā sarvam idaṁ vibhāti*

**“The sun does not shine there (in Brahman), neither does the moon. There the stars do not beam and lightning does not exist, so how could fire be present? All these shine because He shines. The entire universe radiates on account of His effulgence” (Katha Upanisad 2.2.15).**

**Punar-uktavad-ābhāsa**

### 7.103

*punar-uktavad-ābhāsaḥ punar-uktavad eva yaḥ (20)*

**Пословный перевод:**

punah-ukta-vat—that is like a repetition; abhasah—a semblance; punah-ukta—a repetition (“what is said again”); vat—like; eva— just; yah—which.

**Перевод:**

**What appears redundant is called punar-uktavad-abhasa (seeming redundancy).**

### 7.104

*tava tanu-śarīra-sadṛśīṁ*  
*kāñcana kanakasya vīrudhaṁ nekṣe*  
*rādhe su-mukhi bhavatyā*  
*mukha-vad anaṅko ’pi śubhrāṁśuḥ*

**Пословный перевод:**

tava—to Your; tanu—thin; sarira—body; sadrsim—similar; kancana—any \[creeper\]; kanakasya—of gold; virudham—creeper; na ikse—I do not see; radhe—O Radha; su-mukhi—O girl with a beautiful face; bhavatyah—of Yours; mukha-vat—like the face; anankah—spotless (immaculate); api—even; subhra-amsuh—the moon (“whose rays are beautiful”).

**Перевод:**

**Radha, I do not see any golden creeper that resembles Your thin body. O girl with a beautiful face, even if the moon were without spots, it still would not compare to Your face.**

**Комментарий:**

Visvanatha Cakravarti: In this verse, the following words are synonymous, but since they are used in a dissimilar sense, there is punar-uktavad-abhasa: (1) tanu and sarira (body), (2) kancana and kanaka (gold), and (3) mukha and vadana (mouth) (Subodhini). Although the actual word vadana is not used in the verse, that sound occurs in “mukha-vad anankah” by combining the vad in mukha-vad with the ana in anankah.

### 7.105

*ayaṁ śabdārtha-niṣṭho ’pi bhavati. yathā,*

**Перевод:**

**Punar-uktavad-abhasa can also be based on both the words and the meanings. For instance:**

*ghana-jalada-rucira sundara-*  
*dhāma mahaḥ-sañcayaugha-liptāśaḥ*  
*vidhur amṛta-kara-kalā-nidhir*  
*eṣa nabhaḥ-puṣkarākāśaḥ*

**Пословный перевод:**

ghana—dense; jalada—like a cloud (or to clouds); rucira—O You who give off, i.e. emit (ra = rati), a luster (ruci)) (or the moon, which gives splendor); sundara—is beautiful; dhama—O you whose body; mahah—of majesty (or of splendor); sancaya— of a multitude; ogha—with a flood; lipta—are covered (or are smeared); asah—whose aspirations (or by whom the directions); vidhuh—Krsna (or the moon); amrta-kara—whose hand is nectar (or whose rays are nectar); kala-nidhih—an ocean of cleverness (or the receptacle of sixteen fractions); esah—this one; nabhah— during Sravana (or in the sky \[of a lake\]); puskara—is like the sky (or is like a \[white\] lotus); a-kasah—whose perfect luster.

**Перевод:**

**\[First interpretation:\]**

**Krsna, Your body is beautiful and glistens like a raincloud. Its perfect luster resembles the sky during the rainy season. Your overwhelming majestic mood prevents You, Vidhu, from revealing Your desires. Your hands are nectar, and You are an ocean of cleverness.**

**\[Second interpretation:\]**

**O moon, your form appears beautiful and gives brilliance to nearby rainclouds. Your splendor is perfect like a white lotus shining in the lake of the sky. You, vidhu, flood the directions with your radiance. Your rays are like nectar, and you have sixteen fractions.**

*atra śabda-vad artho ’pi punar-uktavad ābhāsate, na tv asya paunaruktyam, nabhāḥ śrāvaṇas tat-sambandhi puṣkaraṁ vyoma, tadvat ā samyak kāśaḥ prakāśo yasya sa tatheti, kṛṣṇa-pakṣe ’nenaiva śyāmatvopalabdheḥ punar ghana-jaladety-ādinā punaruktavat śyāmatvam ity arthaḥ pratibhāsate, na tu punar-uktaḥ. vastutas tu nabhaḥ-puṣkarākāśatvasya sādhyasya ghana-jaladetyādi hetu-bhūtam. evaṁ candra-pakṣe ’pi. tenokta-rūpa-śabdaparivṛtti-vṛttāv api vidhur iti nānārthasya śabdasya sthitau tathāvidhārthālaṅkārasya sthitatvād arthālaṅkārasya prādhānyam.*

**Перевод:**

**In this verse, even the meanings appear to be redundant, like the words do, but there is no redundancy. \[For instance, usually the words nabhas, puskara, and akasa are synonyms of “sky,” therefore using any two of them would seem redundant.\] Here nabhas means the month of Sravana, puskara means the sky, and akasa means: “He whose luster (kasa = prakasa) is perfect (a).” Thus the compound nabhah-puskarakasa means: “He whose luster is perfect like the sky in Sravana.”**

**\[The above is an explanation in regard to individual words, as before, but the following explanation relates to the overall meaning of each of the two compounds:\]**

**When this verse refers to Krsna, the meaning “Krsna is dark blue” that comes from the meaning of the compound ghana- jalada-rucira (lustrous like a dense cloud) seems redundant because the idea that He is dark blue is already obtained with the word nabhah-puskarakasa, but it is not redundant. In truth, Krsna’s being lustrous like a raincloud is the reason that proves the proposition to be proved, namely His being nabhah- puskarakasa (being lustrous like the sky in Sravana) (Sravana is a month in the rainy season (mid-July to mid-August); thus the sky in Sravana is dark blue because of the presence of rainclouds). The same understanding applies to the meanings related to the moon.**

**Therefore an ornament of meaning is predominant here, since even if the aforementioned words were substituted, that ornament of meaning, as expounded above, would remain, so long as the word vidhu, which has diverse meanings (Krsna, moon), remains.**

**Комментарий:**

Punar-uktavad-abhasa is an ubhaya alankara (both an ornament of meaning and an ornament of sound): The word that could be changed is the aspect as an ornament of meaning (as such it resembles artha-slesa), and the word that could not be changed is the aspect as an ornament of sound.

In addition, here Kavi Karnapura mixes punar-uktavad-abhasa with sabda-slesa, insofar as the word vidhu denotes both Krsna and the moon, so that the adjectives are paronomastic. As a result, the aspect as an ornament of meaning becomes an artha-slesa proper: Whichever word in the verse is not a sabda-slesa is an artha-slesa.

In the verse, both the meanings of individual words and the meanings of compounds seem redundant yet they are not so. Just as the individual words ghana and jalada (cloud), rucira and sundara (beautiful), dhama and mahas (splendor), sancaya and ogha (multitude), vidhu, amrta-kara, and kala-nidhi (the moon), and nabhas, puskara, and akasa (sky) seem to be redundant when in fact they are not, since only one term is used in the meaning of a synonym here, so the compounds ghana-jalada-rucira and nabhah-puskarakasa seemingly convey the sense of “being dark blue” when actually they are in a relation of “proof, and the proposition to be proved,” thus there is no actual redundancy.

Kavi Kamapura’s concept of a seeming redundancy of the respective meanings of compounds is an innovation in poetical theory, and so is his explanation along the lines of inference (with regard to hetu and sadhya, “the proof and the proposition to be proved”): This can be classed as the kavya-linga ornament (explanatory reason).

Further, the poetical rhetorician Piyusa-varsa Jayadeva (not the Jayadeva who wrote Glta-govinda) shows this verse as an example of a seeming redundancy where the sounds that make the punar- ukiavad-abhasa are not juxtaposed. In the first half of the verse he defines the ornament:

*punarukta-pratīkāśaṁ*  
*punaruktārtha-sannibham*  
*aṁśu-kāntaṁ śaśī kurvann*  
*ambarāntam upaity asau*

punah-ukta—of a repetition (“what is said again”); pratlkasam—a resemblance; punah-ukta-artha—a meaning that is said again; sannibham—like; amsu—by means of rays; kantam—beauty; sasl—the moon; kurvan—while making; ambara—of the sky (or of the garment); antam—the middle; upaiti—goes; asau—it.

**“A seeming redundancy is what seems like a redundant meaning: “While making beauty with its rays, the moon reaches the middle of the sky”” (Candraloka 5.7).**

The punar-uktavad-abhasa here is founded on a part of a word: In reference to amsu-kantam and ambarantam, it seems that the word antam is repeated.

In addition, there is a semblance of paronomasia (slesabhasa): It’s as if amsu-kantam (beauty with the rays) means amsuka-antam (the inside of the blouse), so that the sense might be: “The moon reaches the inside of the garment (ambara-antam) while making the inside of the blouse.”

The term slesabhasa was coined by Mammata in his analysis of

Udbhata’s methodology of slesa, but Mammata himself did not exemplify it. Rudrata, however, categorizes such a play on words in the category called asambhava-slesa (impossible pun) (Kavyalankara 10.16).

*ity alaṅkāra-kaustubhe śabdālaṅkāra-nirṇayo nāma saptamaḥ kiraṇaḥ.*

**Перевод:**

**Here ends the seventh ray in Alankara-kaustubha, called: “a disquisition on ornaments of sound.”**

## Eighth Ray - Ornaments of Meaning

**1. Upama**

### 8.1

*yathā-kathañcit sādharmyam upamā (1ab)*

**Пословный перевод:**

yatha-kathancit—somehow or other; sadharmyam—sameness of attribute; upama—called upama (simile).

**Перевод:**

**Upama (simile) consists in a similarity of attribute, somehow or other.**

*upamānopameyayor yathā-kathañcid yena kenāpi samānena dharmeṇa sambandha upamā. sa cāṁśena, na tu sarvair aṁśaiḥ— sarvāṁśatvenābhedād upamānopameya-bhāva eva na bhavatīti.*

**Перевод:**

**Upama is the relationship between the upamana (standard of comparison) and the upameya (subject of the comparison) that occurs on account of some attribute in common. The similarity is partial. It is not that all the aspects of the upamana and of the upameya have to be the same because then there could be no relationship between the upamana and the upameya since they would be totally nondifferent.**

**Комментарий:**

Visvanatha Cakravarti explains the term yatha-kathancit (somehow or other): eka-dvy-adi-dharmena na tu sakalena dharmenety arthah, “The similarity is due to either one, two, or more attributes, but not with all attributes” (Subodhini).

Visvanatha Kaviraja defines an attribute in two ways: dharmo guna-kriya-rupah, “An attribute is either a quality or an action” (Sahitya-darpana 10.48).

The purport is that the term yatha-kathancit in the definition does not prevent a simile from occurring when the only similarity is a paronomastic adjective. The concept of yatha-kathancit in the definition of upama originates from Dandi. According to Dr. Belvalkar, the term yatha-kathancit signifies that the similarity can be invented by the poet: It does not have to be real.

The theory on simile, expounded below, is technical. The other ornaments are not so intricate.

### 8.2

*sā bhaved dvidhā (1b)*

*sā upamā.*

**Пословный перевод:**

sa—it (upama); bhavet—is; dvidha—two kinds.

**Перевод:**

**There are two kinds of simile.**

### 8.3

*pūrṇā lupteti pūrṇā tu*  
*dharmeṇaiva yathādibhiḥ (1cd)*  
*upamānopameyābhyām (2a)*

**Пословный перевод:**

purna—complete; lupta—elliptical; iti—namely; purna—complete; tu—but; dharmena—with the common quality; yatha-adibhih— with a word such as yatha; upamana-upameyabhyam—and with the upamana and upameya.

**Перевод:**

**The two varieties of simile are: (1) complete and (2) elliptical.**

**An upama is complete when the four elements are expressed: the upameya, the upamana, the common attribute, and a word of comparison.**

*dharmaḥ sāmānya-dharma āhlādakatvādi. iva-yathā-vādayā aupamya-vācakāḥ. upamānaṁ candrādi. upameyaṁ mukhādi. etair yuktā pūrṇety arthaḥ.*

**Перевод:**

**For example: “Her face is delightful like the moon.” Here the upameya is the face, the upamana is the moon, the attribute in common is “being delightful”, and the word of comparison is “like”. This simile is complete because the four constituent elements are expressed.**

### 8.4

*iyam eveva-vādibhiḥ yuktā śrautī (2bc)*

**Пословный перевод:**

iyam—this (complete upama); eva—only; iva-va-adibhih—with the words iva, va, and so on; yukta—endowed; srautl called srautl (perceived with the ears, i.e. direct).

**Перевод:**

**A complete upama is called direct when the word of comparison is iva, va, yatha, and so on.**

*iyam eva pūrṇā iva-yathā-vādibhir yuktā ced bhavati tadā śrautī. tatra tasyeva ity anena vihito vatiś ca śrautyām eva.*

**Перевод:**

**The suffix vat\[i\] ordained in the rule tatra tasyeva (AstadhyayT 5.1.116) is included in the category of direct simile.**

**Комментарий:**

Jiva Gosvami formulated Panini’s sutra as: tatreva tasyeva va, “Vat\[i\] is also applied in the meanings “like the X in that place” and “like the X of this”” (Hari-namamrta-vyakarana 1198). Examples are shown ahead. The letter in square brackets is used by grammarians to avoid confusion in directly referring to the suffix in writing. On occasion such an additional letter conveys grammatical significance. but in English transliteration often the square brackets are not shown.

### 8.5

*samādyais tu sā syād ārthī ca (2cd)*

**Пословный перевод:**

sama-adyaih—with the words sama and so on; tu—but; sa—that \[complete upama\]; syat—is; arthi—called arthi (implied from the meaning, i.e. indirect).

**Перевод:**

**However, a complete upama is considered indirect when the word of comparison is sama, and so on.**

*sā pūrṇā samādyair yuktā yadi bhavati tadārthī. samādayas tu sama-samāna-sadṛśa-sadṛkṣa-sadṛk-tulya-sammita-nibha-caurabandhu-prabhṛtayaḥ. tena tulyaṁ kriyā ced vatir ity anena vihitena vatinā cārthī. tatra tena tulyam iti tac-chabda upamāna-paraḥ. tulya-śabda upameya-paraḥ. tasya tulyam ity atra viparyayaḥ. ubhayaṁ tulyam ity ubhaya-niṣṭhaḥ.*

**Перевод:**

**The list of words beginnning from sama are: sama, samana, sadrsa, sadrksa, sadrs, tulya, sammita, nibha, caura, bandhu, and so on. The suffix vat\[i\] ordained in tena tulyam kriya ced vatih (AstadhyayT5.1.115) is included in the category of indirect simile. Moreover, when we say tena tulyam, the word tad (tena) refers to the upamana and the word tulya to the upameya. However, when we say tasya tulyam, it’s the opposite (the word tad (tasya) refers to the upameya and the word tulya to the upamana), and when we say ubhayam tulyam then the word ubhaya refers to both the upamana and the upameya.**

**Комментарий:**

The technical difference between iva and so on and sama, tulya, and so on is this: iva and so on express samya (sameness of a common attribute): va va yatha tathevaivam samye, “Va, va, yatha, tatha, iva, and evam are used in the sense of sameness” (Amara-kosa 3.4.9), whereas sama, tulya and so on convey the sense of sadrsya (similarity): vacya-lingah samas tulyah sadrksah sadrsah sadrk, sadharanah samanas ca (Amara-kosa 2.10.37).

Jiva Gosvami explains the usage of vat\[i\] in an indirect complete simile: upamana-kriyad vatis tat-kriya-tulya-kriyatve, “When a similarity between an action and the action which is the standard of comparison is being expressed, vat\[i\] is applied after the person or thing connected with the action which is the standard of comparison” (HNV 1197).

Regarding expressions such as tena tulyam, the word tulya can be replaced with sama and the like. The wording balaramah krsnena tulyah means “Balarama is similar to Krsna”, the wording balaramah krsnasya tulyah means “Krsna is similar to Balarama”, and krsno balaramas ca tulyah means “Krsna and Balarama are alike.” This applies in poetics. In grammar, however, no distinction is made between the third case ending and the sixth case ending, by the rule: tulyarthaih sasthi ca (HNV 677) (tulyarthair atulopamabhyam trtiyanyatarasyam, Astadhyayi 2.3.72).

### 8.6

*taddhite (2d)*  
*vākye samāse cety ete ṣoḍhā (3a)*

**Пословный перевод:**

taddhite—in a word ending in a taddhita suffix; vakye—in a sentence; samase—in a compound word; ca—and; iti—thus; ete— these two (direct and indirect complete upamas); sodha—sixfold.

**Перевод:**

**The complete simile has a total of six varieties since the direct simile and the indirect simile take place either in a taddhita suffix, in a sentence, or in a compound.**

*ete śrauty ārthī ca taddhitādi-trike ṣaḍ-vidhā bhavati. taddhitaṁ tu vaty-ādi. tad yathā—vati-kalpa-deśya-deśīya-bahuc-prabhṛtayaḥ. vākyaṁ prasiddham, samāsaś ca. taddhita-gā śrautī, vākya-gā śrautī, samāsa-gā śrautī, taddhita-gārthī, vākya-gārthī, samāsagārthīti pūrṇā ṣaḍ eva.*

**Перевод:**

**The taddhita suffixes referred to here are vat\[i\], kalpa, desya, desiya, bahu\[c\], and so on. Everyone knows what a sentence (vakya) is and what a compound (samasa) is.**

**Thus the six kinds of complete upama are:**

**1.   taddhita-ga srauti (direct simile in a taddhita suffix),**

**2.   vakya-ga srauti (direct simile in a sentence),**

**3.   samasa-ga srauti (direct simile in a compound),**

**4.   taddhita-garthi (indirect simile in a taddhita suffix),**

**5.   vakya-garthi (indirect simile in a sentence), and**

**6.   samasa-garthi (indirect simile in a compound).**

**Комментарий:**

The rules governing the suffixes kalpa, desya, and desiya are: isad- asamaptau kalpa-desya-desiyah. vaisnava-kalpah. \[...\] akhyatac ca. bhajati-kalpam, “Kalpa, desya, and desiya are used when the accomplishment is somewhat less. For example: vaisnava-kalpah (almost a Vaisnava). They are also used after a verb: bhajati-kalpam (it almost worships)” (HNV Brhat 3080-3081).

Other examples are mrdu-desyah (not quite soft), and pacati- kalpah (he cooks in a manner that is not fully effective) (Kasika 5.3.67). The rule that covers bahu\[c\] is: sv-ady-antat prag bahur va kalparthe. laghur bahu-trnam narah. pakse narayana-kalpa, “Optionally, in the sense of kalpa, bahu can be applied. It is placed before a declined noun: laghuh bahu-trnam narah (a man almost as small as grass); an example of the other option is narayana-kalpa laksmih (Laksmi is almost like Narayana)” (HNV Brhat 3082). Another instance is bahu-patu (quite clever) (Laghu-kaumudi 5.3.68).

### 8.7

*luptā tu lopataḥ*  
*dharma-vādy-upamānānām*

**Пословный перевод:**

lupta—elliptical; tu—but; lopatah—because of the ellipsis; dharma—of the common quality; va-adi—of the word of comparison such as va; upamananam—and of the object of comparison; eka- dvi-tri-kramena—by way of one, two, or three; hi—only.

Ahead, Kavi Karnapura mentions the elliptical simile which involves the elision of the upameya.

dharma-lope—when there is an ellipsis of the common quality; kramena—in order; esa—this \[elliptical upama\]; purna-vat—like the complete one; sad-vidha—of six kinds; udita—is said; kintu— but; taddhita-ga srauti—the taddhita-ga srauti variety; luptayam— in an elliptical upama; na—not; iti—thus; pancadha—five kinds.

*eṣā luptā taddhita-gādi-bhedena pūrṇāvat ṣaḍ-vidhā bhavitum ucitā. śrautī luptā tri-vidhā, ārthī luptā tri-vidheti. kintu dharmalopa-taddhita-gā śrautī luptā na bhavatīti pañcaiva—vākya-gā śrautī luptā, samāsa-gā śrautī luptā, taddhita-gārthī luptā, vākyagārthī luptā, samāsa-gārthī lupteti.*

**Перевод:**

**3.   taddhita-garthi lupta (indirect simile in a taddhita suffix),**

**4.   vakya-garthi lupta (indirect simile in a sentence), and,**

**5.   samasa-garthi lupta (indirect simile in a compound).**

**6.  Utprekṣā**

### 8.58

*sambhāvanopamānenopameyotkarṣa-hetukā*  
*utprekṣā nūnam ity-ādi-śabda-dyotyā (15abcd)*

**Пословный перевод:**

sambhavana—imagination; upamanena—by means of the object of comparison; upameya—of the subject of the comparison; utkarsa—is the elevation; hetuka—whose purpose; utpreksa— poetical fancy; nunam iti-adi—nunam and so on; sabda—by the words; dyotya—indicated.

**Перевод:**

**Utpreksa is a fanciful assumption for the sake of exalting the upameya through the upamana. It is indicated by the word nunam and so on.**

*utprekṣā-nāmālaṅkāraḥ. sambhāvanā hetv-antaropanyāsena vitarkanam. nūnaṁ-manye-śaṅke-iva-dhruvaṁ-nu-kiṁ-kimutetyādayo nūnam-ādayaḥ.*

**Перевод:**

**Sambhavana is an assumption by inserting another reason (usually an imagined attribute). The words that signal an utpreksa are: nunam (surely), manye (I think), sanke (I suspect, I guess), iva (as if), dhruvam (for sure), nu (perhaps), kim (whether), kim uta (whether or), and so on.**

**Комментарий:**

In English rhetoric, utpreksa corresponds to conceit. A simple instance of utpreksa is: nunam tasya mukham candrah, “Surely, her face is a moon.” If the imagination is blatant, a word expressive of utpreksa is not required, but sometimes such a wording fits in a category of the virodha ornament (contradiction) (8.168). Moreover, the difference between the usage of the word iva in a simile and its usage in an utpreksa is that the latter involves a fanciful imagination.

There are various ways of constructing an utpreksa. All ornaments that consist of a comparison are meant to exalt the upameya

(subject of the comparison), also called prakrta (or prastuta, the subject of description). Often, the particularity of utpreksa is that the upamana is imagined to have a fanciful attribute. Dr. Kane comments: “Appaya-dikshita bases the difference upon the existence of adjectives or attributes that would contribute towards the poetic representation of the identity of the prakrta and aprakrta.”

In that regard, Nagesa Bhatta explains the derivation: utkata prakrstasyopamanasyeksa jnanam utpreksa, “Utpreksa is an over- the-top (ut = utkata) perception (iksa = jnanam) of an eminent standard of comparison (pra = prakrstasya upamanasya)” (Uddyota 10.92). But sometimes an utpreksa does not involve a comparison.

*nānyo hetus tad iha lalite vīkṣya vīkṣya tvad-āsyaṁ*  
*nūnaṁ dhātā tam aticaturo nirmimīte ’numāsam*

**Пословный перевод:**

nastah nastah—disappears; prati-kuhu—on every new moon (amavasya); muhuh—again; purnatam—fullness; eti—attains; candrah—the moon; rakam rakam prati—on every purnima; na— not; tu—but; bhavet—is; anya-rupah—having a different form; kada api—at any time; na—not; anyah—other; hetuh—reason; tat—therefore; iha—in this regard; lalite—O Lalita; viksya viksya— after seeing again and again; tvat-asyam—your face; nunam— certainly; dhata—the creator; tam—it (the moon); aticaturah— very intelligent; nirmimite—creates; anumasam—every month.

**Перевод:**

**The moon disappears on every Amavasya and again attains fullness on every Purnima. It never has another form. The other reasons are not true. Therefore, Lalita, it must be that the intelligent creator, repeatedly contemplating on your face, recreates the moon every month.**

**Комментарий:**

Visvanatha Cakravarti: The implied meaning is this: After creating the entire world, the creator beheld Lalita’s face and desired to create something similar to it. Thus, from amavasya up until purnima, he set to work creating the full moon. But then, seeing that the full moon didn’t compare to Lalita’s face, out of frustration, he began to destroy it little by little beginning from pratipat. In this way, he removed all trace of the full moon by amavasya, and from amavasya he began again to create another moon, hoping that it would resemble Lalita’s face. Even now the creator does this. His attempts have not ceased (Subodhinl).

In other words, during the new moon, people assume that the moon retains its form and can be seen from another part of the globe; however, here the poet’s intention is to express that the moon simply does not exist on Amavasya because the creator completely eradicates it. The utpreksa consists in imagining that the moon has the aforesaid mode of being.

**Перевод:**

**As if out of kindness, the moon extinguishes with its rays the fire of intense separation felt by the night-blooming lotuses, whose mouths open as they begin to yawn. Thus the moon extricates the ensnared bumblebees, which look like piles of charcoal.**

**Комментарий:**

Visvanatha Cakravarti: The exchange between the night-blooming lotuses and the bees is as follows: At night, the night-blooming lotuses are open and bumblebees enter them to drink their flower nectar, but when those lotuses close upon seeing the sun, the bumblebees get stuck inside. The verse features two expressed utpreksas: (1) krpaya iva (as if out of kindness), and (2) angara-punjam iva (they look like piles of charcoal).

**8.  Rūpaka**

### 8.66

**Перевод:**

**Комментарий:**

The name rupaka is appropriate, as in it the visayi (aropyamana or upamana) imposes its form (rupa) on the visaya (aropa-visaya or upameya). In this regard, Ruyyaka says: visayina visayasya rupavatah karanad rupakam, “Rupaka is so named because the visayimakes the visaya possess its form” (Alankara-sarvasva). For example, in mukha-candrah (moon face), the moon, the upamana (standard of comparison), makes the face, the upameya, possess its shape.

In this variety of rupaka, there is a main metaphor, and corresponding subordinate metaphors are built upon it, thus the metaphors collectively paint a whole picture. For example, here the main metaphor is tanu-ratna-latika (a jewelled creper in the form of a body). The upamana is the creeper, and the upameya is Radha’s body. Upon this main metaphor are built the following subordinate metaphors: (1) udancad-vaksoja-stavaka (the bunches of flowers in the form of raised breasts), (2) bahu-vitapa-dvaya (a pair of branches in the form of arms), (3) smita-kusuma-saurabhya (the fragrance of the flower in the form of a smile), and (4) mrdu- pany-anguli-dala (leaves in the form of fingers of the soft hand).

**Paramparita-rūpaka**

### 8.79

*śliṣṭasya vācakasyānurodhād āropa eva yaḥ*  
*so ’nyasyāropa-hetuś cet paramparita-nāmakam (19)*

**Пословный перевод:**

slistasya—which has a double meaning; vacakasya—of a word; anurodhat—due to the compatibility; aropah—superimposition; eva—only; yah—which; sah—that; anyasya—of another; aropa- hetuh—the cause of the superimposition; cet—if; paramparita— chain; namakam—called.

**Перевод:**

**If, due to the compatibility of a word that has a double meaning, one superimposition is the cause of the superimposition of something else, then the rupaka is called paramparita (serial metaphors, i.e. one metaphor causes the other).**

*anyasyāśliṣṭasyārope yadi hetuḥ syāt tadā rūpakaṁ paramparitākhyam.*

**Перевод:**

**If a rupaka is the cause of the superimposition of another thing which does not have a double meaning, then it is called paramparita.**

**Комментарий:**

The word paramparita (it has a series) is formed like tarakita (it has stars), by the rule: tadasya sanjatam tarakadibhya itac (Astadhyayi 5.2.36). Vidyadhara derives paramparita as: parampara jatasyeti paramparitam, “A succession has occurred in relation to this (in relation to rupaka)” (Ekavali 8.28).

### 8.80

*yathā,*  
*padmānanotsukatayā bhramaraḥ kalābhiḥ*  
*sarvābhir anvitatayā tvam akhaṇḍa induḥ*  
*tvan-mānase kanaka-paṅkajinītayāsau*  
*sā rādhikā suramaṇī-nikārādhikaiva*

**Пословный перевод:**

padma—of the goddess of fortune (or, padma—lotus); anana—for the face; utsukataya—because of being eager; bhramarah—a bee; kalabhih—with the sixty-four arts (or, with the sixteen digits of the moon); sarvabhih—all anvitataya—because of being endowed; tvam—You; akhandah—full; induh—moon; tvat—Your; manase— in the mind (or, in the lake); kanaka—golden; pankajinltaya— because of being a lotus; asau—that; sa—well-known; radhika— Radhika (or, sara-adhika—greater in terms of excellence); su- ramanl—of beautiful young women; nikara—than the multitude; adhika—greater; eva—only.

**Перевод:**

**Krsna, You are a bee because You are very eager for the face of Padma, You are a full moon because You are endowed with all the kalas, and Radhika, who is well-known (sa radhika), is greater (sara-adhika) than all other beautiful girls because She is a golden lotus on the Manasa Lake of Your mind.**

*atra padmaṁ padmā ca, kalāś catuḥṣaṣṭi, kalā candrasya ṣoḍaśo bhāgaś ca, mānasaṁ cittaṁ mānasa-saraś ca, sā rādhikā sāreṇādhikā sārādhikā, ity eṣāṁ śliṣṭānāṁ vācakānām anurodhāt bhramarādi-śabdānām āropaḥ.*

**Перевод:**

**In the compound padmanana, the first word can be either padma (lotus) or padma (the goddess of fortune). Kala can denote the sixty-four arts or the sixteen phases of the moon. Manasa refers to the mind and to the lake, and sa radhika can also be read saradhika (sara-adhika), which means sarenadhika (greater (adhika) in terms of excellence (sarena). Consequently, due to the compatibility of these words, which have double meanings, there is a superimposition of the bee and so on upon Krsna.**

**Комментарий:**

Paramparita-rupaka is caused either by a paronomastic word (a one-word metaphor) or by nonparonomastic words. This verse exemplifies the former. For instance, the word padmanana means “The face of Laksmi is the face (whorl) of a lotus.” The superimposition of the lotus upon Laksmi is the cause of the superimposition of the bee upon Krsna. Thus the Krsna bee is eager for the Laksmi lotus.

The other explanations are: (1) The superimposition of the sixteen phases of the moon upon the sixty-four arts, occasioned by the double meaning on kala, is the cause of the superimposition of the full moon upon Krsna, and (2) The superimposition of the lake upon the mind, which occurs due to the double meaning on manasa (His mind is a Manasa Lake), is the cause of the superimposition of a golden lotus upon Radhika. Thus here slesa is the anga and rupaka the angi (8.300). In addition, the one-word metaphor is implied.

### 8.82

*yathā,*  
*ratna-stambhau vraja-mṛgadṛśāṁ citta-dolotsavasya*  
*śrī-rādhāyā rati-jaya-kalā-toraṇottāna-daṇḍau*  
*daityendrānāṁ paribhava-mahā-yajña-nīlendra-yūpau*  
*śuṇḍe kāma-pramada-kariṇoḥ kṛṣṇa-bāhū smarāmaḥ*

**Пословный перевод:**

ratna-stambhau—two jewelled pillars; vraja-mrgadrsam—of the doe-eyed girls of Vraja; citta—of the hearts; dola—in the form of the swinging; utsavasya—for the festival; sri-radhayah—of Sri Radha; rati—of love; jaya—of the superexcellence; kala—in the form of the expertise; torana—for the festoons of leaves suspended across gateways; uttana-dandau—two upraised poles; daitya-indranam— of the chiefs of demons; paribhava—in the form of the conquering; maha-yajna—in the great sacrifice; nilendra—sapphire; yupau— two sacrificial posts; sunde—two trunks; kama-pramada—in the forms of lust and joy; karinoh—of the two elephants; krsna- bahu—upon the two arms of Krsna; smaramah—we remember (we meditate).

**Перевод:**

**Let us meditate upon Krsna’s two arms. They are the two jewelled pillars for the swing festival of the hearts of the doe­eyed girls of Vraja, the two raised poles from which hangs the festoon of Radha’s superexcellent love, the two sapphire sacrificial posts in the great sacrifice of conquering the chiefs of evil beings, and the trunks of the two elephants of lust and joy.**

*atra citta-dolanāder bhinna-śabda-vācyasyotsavādy-āropeṇa bāhvo ratna-stambhatvādy-āropaḥ siddha eva. ādyayor miśratvam, uttarayoḥ śuddhatvam.*

**Перевод:**

**Here the superimposition of the festival and so on upon the swinging of the heart and so on, which is expressed in separate words, is the cause of the superimposition of the jewelled pillars, etc., upon the arms, and so on. In this verse, the first two paramparita rupakas are mixed whereas the last two are pure.**

**Комментарий:**

There are four paramparita rupakas in the verse: (1) The superimposition of a festival upon the swinging of the heart is the cause of the superimposition of the jewelled pillars upon the arms (the arms are pillars), (2) The superimposition of a festoon upon Radha’s superexcellent love is the cause of the superimposition of the poles upon the arms, (3) The superimposition of a great sacrifice upon the conquering of the chiefs of evil beings is the cause of the superimposition of the sacrificial posts upon the arms, and (4) The superimposition of elephants upon lust and joy is the cause of the superimposition of trunks upon the arms.

These effected metaphors are not based upon the compatibility of words which have double meanings, rather the swinging of the heart and so on are all expressed in separate words.

The whole verse also illustrates mala-rupaka (series of metaphors): In the enumeration, the first two paramparita rupakas are pure in the sense that the common attribute is the same (8.42): Both jewelled pillars and poles have the common quality of supporting.

### 8.90

*śliṣṭair viśeṣaṇair eva*

**Пословный перевод:**

slistaih—which are paronomastic; visesanaih—with adjectives (modifiers); eva—only; visesyasya—of the main noun; anyatha- sthitih—appearing otherwise; samasa-uktih—the ornament called samasokti.

**Перевод:**

**When a noun appears to refer to something else due to parono- mastic adjectives, that is samasokti (concise statement).**

*viśeṣyasya kevalasya śliṣṭair viśeṣaṇair anyathā-sthitir*  
*anyathābhāsanaṁ samāsokti-nāmālaṅkāraḥ.*

**Перевод:**

**When a noun, which has only one meaning, appears to refer to something else due to modifiers which have double meanings, that is the ornament called samasokti.**

**Комментарий:**

If the noun were paronomastic, the text would be a slesa (sabda- slesa) and would occasion an implied simile. Moreover, samasokti is the opposite of aprastuta-prasamsa insofar as in samasokti, the prastuta (subject of description) implies an aprastuta (what is not the actual subject of description), whereas in aprastuta-prasamsa the reverse occurs.

**There are five kinds of aprastuta-prasamsa: An effect, a cause, a general situation or a specific situation is the contextual topic (prastuta), but instead there is talk of a noncontextual topic (aprastuta); and when a meaning is contextual (prastuta), but there is talk of a similar thing (aprastuta) instead.**

*tad aprastuta-praśaṁsanaṁ prastuteṣu kāryādiṣu tad-anya-gīḥ kāraṇādi-niruktiḥ, ca-kārād anyeṣām aprastutatva-prasaṅgaḥ. tulye prastute tulyasyāprastutasya gīś ceti pañcadhā. kārye kāraṇakathanam, kāraṇe kārya-kathanam, sāmānye viśeṣa-kathanam, viśeṣe sāmānya-kathanam, tulye tulyasyāprastutasya kathanam ity arthaḥ.*

**Перевод:**

**The five varieties are: (1) Talking about a cause when an effect is the subject matter, (2) Talking about an effect when a cause is the subject matter, (3) Talking about a specific situation when a general situation is the subject matter, (4) Talking about a general situation when a specific situation is the subject matter, and (5) A topic is the subject matter, but instead there is talk of a similar thing which is not contextual.**

**14.  Atiśayokti**

**Комментарий:**

There are four kinds of atisayokti. The first kind, defined above, was described in text 2.22. This variety amounts to an extreme metaphor: The intent is to express an utter nondifference between the upameya and the upamana. The superimposition is so complete that there is no longer any apprehension of the upameya, therefore the upameya is not stated at all.

The atisayokti which is “a statement of superexcellence”, mentioned in the third chapter (23; 42; 49), is the ancients’ atisayokti and more or less corresponds to the second kind (8.116-117).

sarvesam—all; eva—the same; dharmanam—of the attributes; drsta-antah—the ornament called drstanta; pratibimba-vat—like a reflection.

**Перевод:**

**When all the attributes in the upameya sentence are in the upamana sentence as if they were being mirrorred, that is the ornament called drstanta (exemplification).**

*sarveṣām eva sādhāraṇa-dharmāṇāṁ pratibimba-vat bhāsanaṁ yat tad dṛṣṭānta-nāmālaṅkāraḥ.*

**Комментарий:**

In prativastupama and in drstanta, two sentences are compared, but a word such as iva (like) is never used. In short,prativastupama is a deficient drstanta. Moreover, Mammata says drstanta is so called because in it the conclusion (anta) is seen (drsta). Govinda Thakkura and Nagesa Bhatta explain that drstanta is so called because in it there is the ascertainment of the meaning of the upameya sentence. Drstanta becomes an ornament when it is poetical.

### 8.128

*krameṇodāharaṇe,*

**Перевод:**

**Two examples are shown in order. \[This verse illustrates sadharmya-drstanta (similarity of qualities):\]**

*hari-sandarśana-samaye*  
*dravati mano me kaṭhoram api su-mukhi*  
*udaye sati candramasaś*  
*candra-maṇeḥ syandate sva-rasaḥ*

**Пословный перевод:**

hari—Hari; sandarsana—of beholding; samaye—at the time; dravati—melts; manah—heart; me—my; kathoram—hard; api—even; su-mukhi—O girl with a beautiful face; udaye sati—when there is the rising; candramasah—of the moon; candra-maneh—of the moon gem (the candrakanta jewel, “which has the effulgence of the moon”); syandate—flows; sva-rasah—the own essence.

**Перевод:**

**Girl with a lovely face, when I gaze at Hari even my hard heart melts. When the moon rises, the candrakanta jewel effuses its essence.**

**Комментарий:**

The candrakanta jewel is said to be formed from the coagulation of moonrays and to dissolve under moonlight. According to Visvanatha Cakravarti, the two qualities, solidity and liquidity, are mirrored in the example. The heart’s softness in Krsna’s presence and its hardness form a parallel with the candrakanta jewel’s softness in the presence of the moon and with its hardness respectively.

The verse illustrates drstanta because all the things are mirrorred: Hari, her heart and the melting of her heart are mirrorred by the moon, the jewel and the jewel’s essence.

Moreover, in arthantara-nyasa (8.165), a general proposition is strengthened by a particular instance or a particular instance is strengthened by a general proposition. However, in prativastupama and in drstanta the two sentences do not stand in the relation of general and particular propositions. In these two ornaments, if the first clause is a particular proposition, the second is so as well.

**Перевод:**

**Darkness enters my eyes when my beloved is far from my eyes. However, blue lotuses do not remain closed when the moon rises.**

**Комментарий:**

There is a parallelism between Krsna and the moon, and Radha’s eyes and blue lotuses. The poetical convention is that blue lotuses open in moonlight. The contrast expressed by the second sentence is: When Krsna arrives in Her presence, Her eyes open.

*yathā,*  
*āloke sati sammadāmṛta-nidhau svāntaṁ tadaivāviśat*

*krūratve ’pi ca tasya dhairya-haratā tasyāṁ samastendriya-*  
*glāniḥ kā sakhi su-sthitābhilaṣati śrī-kṛṣṇam ālokitum*

**Пословный перевод:**

aloke sati—when there is seeing \[Krsna\]; sammada—of exhilaration; amrta-nidhau—in the nectar ocean; svantam—the heart; tada—then; eva—only; avisat—entered (i.e. enters); svante— in the heart; manmathah—Cupid; esah—this; manmathe—in Cupid; idam—this; kruratvam—anger; uccaih-taram—abundantly; kruratve—in anger; api—even; ca—and; tasya—his (i.e. Cupid’s); dhairya—patience; harata—quality of destroying; tasyam— in that \[destruction of patience\]; samasta-indriya—of all the senses; glanih—the dwindling; ka—which girl; sakhi—O friend; su-sthita—being properly situated (i.e. being in her right mind); abhilasati—longs; sri-krsnam—Sri Krsna; alokitum—to see.

Here the verb avisat (entered) is stated once and is carried forward in each clause. The verse is a form of mala because there is a series and features dipaka because the verb, situated in one place, illumines the things connected to it. The term dipaka means either (1) “Illuminator”: The suffix \[n\]aka is applied after the verbal root dip\[i\] diptau (to illuminate), (2) “A small lamp”: The small ka\[n\] is applied in the sense of smallness, by the rule: alpe (Astadhyayi 5.3.85), or (3) “Like a lamp”: The suffix ka\[n\] is applied after dipa (lamp) in the sense of iva (like), as in the poetical term yamaka (word rhyme) (“like a pair”), by the rule: ivepratikrtau (Astadhyayi 5.3.96).

### 8.138

*yathā,*  
*dṛṣṭaṁ śrī-kṛṣṇa-vadanaṁ hāritaṁ ca nijaṁ manaḥ*  
*labdhaḥ ko ’pi parānando nipītaṁ ca mahā-viṣam*

**Пословный перевод:**

drstam—has been seen; sri-krsna-vadanam—Sri Krsna’s face; haritam—was stolen; ca—and; nijam—my; manah—mind; labdhah—has been obtained; kah api—some; para-anandah— great bliss; nipitam—has been drunk; ca—and; maha-visam—huge poison.

**Перевод:**

**Ah, I saw Sri Krsna’s face and my mind was blown away; I experienced some great bliss and I drunk a powerful poison.**

**Комментарий:**

Visvanatha Cakravarti says that an equal connection with the word ca is understood here: Krsna’s face was seen and the mind was blown away (Subodhini). However, a similarity must be implied, otherwise the verse would be same as the variety of samuccaya consisting of a combination of two actions (8.216). This subvariety of tulya-yogita is not distinguished from samuccaya simply by the usage of the word ca, because the poets use that formula for samuccaya. Here the implied similarities are: “Seeing Krsna’s face is the same as having one’s mind blown away,” and “Experiencing bliss connected with Krsna is like drinking poison \[due to not being able to meet Him\].”

Kavi Karnapura mentioned this variety of tulya-yogita in text 3.55. According to Mammata, this is actually a tulyayogita-dhvani. In his chapter on first-rate poetry, he writes: atra tulya-yogita- dyotakasya ‘ca’ iti nipatasya, “Here the particle ca (and) hints at the tulya-yogita ornament” (Kavya-prakasa, verse 108 vrtti). This is the verse:

*kṛtaṁ ca garvābhimukhaṁ manas tvayā*  
*kim anyad evaṁ nihatāś ca no dviṣaḥ*  
*tamāṁsi tiṣṭhanti hi tāvad aṁśumān*  
*na yāvad āyāty udayādri-maulitām*

**“You made your mind intent on showing arrogant pride and, what’s more, our enemies were struck down. Darkness remains so long as the sun does not reach the eastern horizon.” (KP verse 108)**

The difference between this tulya-yogita and the samuccaya ornament is that here a similarity is implied: “Making your mind intent on showing arrogant pride equals striking our enemies.” Nagesa Bhatta says this is called tulya-yogita simply because two things happen at the same time (tulya = tulya-kala) (there is no causal relation): tulya-kalam yogiteti vyutpattya tulya- yogita-sabdenoktah (Uddyota on Kavya-prakasa verse 108). In addition, Nagesa Bhatta remarks that the second sentence of the verse illustrates vyatireka-drstanta (contrasted example): tatra vyatirekena drstantam aha tamamsi (Uddyota).

Pandita-raja Jagannatha uses the word ca in tulya-yogita, but he mentions the point in common:

*priye viṣādaṁ jahihīti vācaṁ*  
*priye sa-rāgaṁ vadati priyāyāḥ*  
*vārām udārā vijagāla dhārā*  
*vilocanābhyāṁ manasaś ca mānaḥ*

**“When the lover told his sweetheart: “Honey, let go of your despondency,” the abundant flow of water from her eyes and the pique from her mind abated” (Rasa-gangadhara).**

The tears and the pique are contextual, since the sulky woman is the subject of description, and share the attribute of abating. Over and above that, Jagannatha means to illustrate an implied similarity. He says it is twofold: The tears and the pique are similar and her eyes and her mind are similar. In other words, “The pique from her mind resembled the tears from her eyes,” otherwise Jagannatha’s example would be classed as the variety of samuccaya consisting of the simultaneous occurrence of two actions.

**20.  Vyatireka**

### 8.139

*vyatireko vilakṣaṇaḥ*  
*upamānāt (33bc)*

**Пословный перевод:**

vyatirekah—the ornament called vyatireka; vilaksanah—difference in characteristics; upamanat—from the object with which something is compared.

**Перевод:**

**When there is a dissimilitude between the upameya (subject of the compasrion) and the upamana (standard of comparison), that is vyatireka (contrast with an implied similitude).**

*vilakṣaṇa iti guṇena doṣeṇa ca.*

**Перевод:**

**The dissimilitude occurs on account of either a quality or a fault.**

**Комментарий:**

Vyatireka is characterized by a contrast between an upameya and an upamana. but there must be some degree of similitude between them. Any contrast not involving an upameya and an upamana is classed as the visama ornament (incongruity) (8.256), and so is a contrast between an upameya and an upamana that does not involve similitude. And if a well-known upamana is taken as an upameya. that is in the scope of the pratlpa ornament (reverse simile) (8.277).

### 8.140

*krameṇodāharaṇāni—“āśā-mātre vilasad-udayaḥ” ity-ādi.*

Examples are shown in order. This is from the third chapter:

**Перевод:**

**May the Krsna moon, by its flood of effulgence, take away the coldness of those who worship Him. (The Krsna moon takes away coolness, i.e. it gives heat, whereas the normal moon gives coolness.) He is the friend ofpadmims. (The Krsna moon is the friend of beautiful women whereas the moon is not the friend of daytime lotuses.) He is always taking pleasure (abhoga). (But the usual moon is full, abhoga, only once a month.) His bliss, friendship, and sweetness are perpetual. (But the moon’s only occur at night.) The Krsna moon is always embracing Radha. (But the moon is only in conjunction with the constellations such as Radha and Aslesa once every twenty-seven days.) Krsna has soft reddish feet (pada). (But the moon’s rays, pada, are white.) He appears splendidly whenever His devotees desire Him (asa). (But the full moon only rises in one direction (asa).) (3.13)**

**Комментарий:**

Vyatireka takes place here because, in terms of good qualities, Krsna, the upameya, is superior to the moon, the upamana.

### 8.141

*yathā vā,*  
*rādhe sudhāṁśur evāyaṁ satyam eva tavānanam*  
*kintv asau malino ’ṅkena su-nirmalam idaṁ sadā*

**Пословный перевод:**

radhe—O Radha; sudha-amsuh—the moon (“whose rays are nectar”); eva—only; ayam—this; satyam—truly; eva—only; tava— Your; ananam—face; kintu—but; asau—that; malinah—dirty; ankena—because of a mark; su-nirmalam—beautiful and blemish- free; idam—this; sada—always.

**Перевод:**

**Radha, in truth Your face is a moon. However, the famous moon is stained because of a mark whereas this moon, Your face, is always beautiful and blemish-free.**

**Комментарий:**

Here also there is a dissimilitude on account of a good quality: Radha’s face, the upameya, is superior to the well-known moon, the upamana. In addition, a fault of the moon is mentioned.

*durāpa-loke ca navānurāgo*  
*hālāhalaṁ cāpi samaṁ viśākhe*  
*antyaṁ tu mantrauṣadhi-ratna-sādhyaṁ*  
*hā hanta kenāpi kadāpi nādyaḥ*

**Пословный перевод:**

durapa-loke—for Krsna (“the seeing of whom is difficult to obtain”); ca—and; nava-anuragah—new love; halahalam—deadly poison; ca—and; api—even; samam—are similar; visakhe—O Visakha; antyam—the last one (poison); tu—but; mantra-osadhi-ratna—by mantras, medicines, and jewels; sadhyam—can be counteracted; ha—alas; hanta—alas; kena api—by any means; kada api—at any time; na—not; adyah—the first one (new love for Krsna).

**Перевод:**

**Visakha, first love for Krsna, seeing whom is hard to achieve, and the halahala poison are similar, but although the latter can be counteracted by mantras, medicines, and jewels, the former cannot be counteracted by any means.**

**Комментарий:**

Visvanatha Cakravarti: First love for Krsna, the upameya, is dissimilar to poison, the upamana, on account of a fault (Subodhim). The fault is that first love for Krsna cannot be counteracted.

### 8.143

*dvayor utkarṣāpakarṣārtha-śaṁsinoḥ (33cd)*  
*hetvor uktau trayāṇāṁ vānuktau śabdārtha-śaktitaḥ*  
*ākṣipte sati ca śleṣe sa syād bahu-vidhaḥ punaḥ (34)*

**Пословный перевод:**

dvayoh—of both \[the upameya and upamana\]; utkarsa—of eminence; apakarsa—of inferiority; artha—the sense; samsinoh— which express; hetvoh—of the attributes \[between the upameya and the upamana\]; uktau—when there is mention; trayanam—of the group of three \[categories (see the vrtti)\]; va—and; anuktau— when there is no mention; sabda—of the words; artha—of the meanings; saktitah—on account of the power; aksipte sati— when there is intimation; ca—and; slese—when there are double meanings; sah—that (vyatireka); syat—is; bahu-vidhah—manifold; punah—furthermore.

**Перевод:**

**Vyatireka is manifold, in consideration of these factors:**

**♦   The mention of the upameya’s and the upamana’s attributes, which reveal their eminence and inferiority respectively,**

**♦   The non-mention (of eminence and inferiority), which has three categories,**

**♦   The power of words and meanings,**

**♦   The similarity is only implied, and**

**♦   Double meanings.**

*dvayor upameyopamānayor upameyasyotkarṣa upamānasyāpakarṣaḥ, tayor uktau dvayor upameyopamānayor utkarṣāpakarṣayor anuktiḥ. upameyasyotkarṣasya vānuktiḥ, upamānasyāpakarṣasya vānuktiḥ, iti tritayaṁ militvā catvāro bhedāḥ. ete ca śabda-pratipāditā artha-pratipāditāś cety aṣṭau. ākṣipte ’py aupamye catvāraḥ. evaṁ dvādaśa. punaḥ śleṣe dvādaśeti caturviṁśati-bhedāḥ.*

**Перевод:**

**When there is a mention of both the eminence of the upameya and the inferiority of the upamana, that is the first variety of vyatireka. There are three other varieties: (2) Neither the eminence of the upameya nor the inferiority of the upamana is mentioned, (3) The eminence of the upameya is not mentioned, and (4) The inferiority of the upamana is not mentioned.**

**This makes four varieties, which become eight since the idea of similarity can be conveyed either by a word or by the meaning (as in the direct and indirect varieties of upama). If the comparison is implied, that makes another four varieties for a total of twelve. And there are twelve more varieties on account of double meanings, for a total of twenty-four varieties of vyatireka.**

*krameṇodāharaṇāni,*

**21.   Ākṣepa**

### 8.154

*ākṣepo vaktum iṣṭasya yo viśeṣa-vivakṣayā*  
*niṣedho vakṣyamāṇatvenoktatvena ca sa dvidhā (35)*  
*sa ākṣepa-nāmālaṅkāraḥ.*

**Пословный перевод:**

aksepah—the ornament called aksepa; vaktum—to be said; istasya— which was intended; yah—which \[denial\]; visesa-vivaksaya— out of a desire to express a special meaning; nisedhah—denial; vaksyamanatvena—according to what is yet to be said; uktatvena— according to what has been said; ca—and; sah—that \[ornament\]; dvidha—is twofold.

**Перевод:**

**When there is an apparent denial of something, which was intended to be said, for the purpose of conveying some special meaning, that is called aksepa (hinting by negating). It has two varieties: What is suppressed is yet to be said (aposiopesis) or has already been said (paralipsis).**

**Комментарий:**

In aksepa, there are four essential characteristics: (1) Something is intended to be said, (2) There must be an expressed denial or suppression of it, (3) This denial or suppression is a mere semblance, and (4) Some special meaning is meant. In aksepa the suggested meaning is subordinate to the expressed sense and is thus a second- rate implied sense.

Visvanatha Cakravarti: There is an antithesis of moonrays as a category and of a conflagration as a category, and similarly of camphor and fire, and sandalwood paste and fire. However, those antitheses are a mere semblance of a contradiction because in separation from Krsna cool substances feel like fire since they are uddlpakas (they cause the ladyloves’ emotions to flare up): Moonrays and so on do not really become fire (Subodhinl). The logical contradiction is removed by the poetical usage.

There are three antitheses in the verse: (1) Cupid, as a category, is incompatible with the quality of being disgusting, (2) The ocean, as a category, is incompatible with the quality of being shallow, and (3) Sumeru mountain, as a category, is incompatible with the quality of being tiny.

In texts 8.177 and 8.178, however, Cupid is taken as a unique entity (dravya). It is a question of perspective: Here Cupid is part of a category of Cupids: The multiplicity of Cupids is accounted for by considering that many universes exist.

*dravyaṁ dravyeṇa. evaṁ daśa bhedāḥ.*

**Перевод:**

**This is an antithesis of a unique entity with another (Cupid cannot become a thunderbolt). The ten varieties of virodha are thus exemplified.**

**Комментарий:**

Here the antithesis between unique things is that Cupid, who is a cause of relishing rasa, cannot become a thunderbolt. In virodha, the strikingness lies more in the contradiction than in the non­difference. Conversely, in rupaka (metaphor) the charm lies more in the non-difference than in the contradiction.

**29.   Sahokti**

### 8.186

*sahoktiḥ sā sahārthena śabdenaikā kriyā yadi (42ab)*

**Пословный перевод:**

saha-uktih—the ornament called sahokti; sa—that; saha-arthena— which has the sense of saha (with); sabdena—with one word; eka—one; kriya—verb; yadi—if.

**Перевод:**

**If a verb is connected with a word that has the sense of saha (with), that is sahokti (connected statement).**

**Комментарий:**

Sahokti means “a mention of saha.”Any word which means ‘with’ can be used. Those words are: saha, samam, sardham, sakam, and sajuh.

In grammar, words such as saha are used in two ways, but only one of the two is used here. The two kinds are:

1\.   The secondary thing only exists with the main thing, as in: “Krsna plays with Balarama” (this is not sahokti), and

2\.   Both the main thing and the secondary thing are equally connected with the action, quality, or object.

Often sahokti takes the form of a pun, but it is not classed as a slesa (artha-slesa) because by definition the word used with saha has a secondary status in the sentence, whereas in artha-slesa both things must be equally predominant: saharthair apradhane trfiya (HNV 676); saha-yukte ’pradhane (Astadhyayi 2.3.19).

**34.  Paryāyokta**

### 8.202

*vinā vācaka-vācyatvaṁ*  
*yatra vastu pratīyate*  
*paryāyoktaṁ tat (46abc)*

**Пословный перевод:**

vina—without; vacaka-vacyatvam—the words’ being literally expressive (vacaka) and the literal meanings expressed (vacya) by the words; yatra—in which; vastu—an idea; pratiyate—is understood; paryaya-uktam—the ornament called paryayokta (a roundabout mode of expression); tat—that.

**Перевод:**

**When an idea is understood even though the words or the meanings do not literally express it, that is paryayokta (periphrasis).**

### 8.203

*jahau śrī-kṛṣṇam ālokya sthitiṁ svābhāvikīm api*  
*darpaḥ kandarpa-hṛdaye māno mānavatī-hṛdi*

**Пословный перевод:**

jahau—relinquished; sri-krsnam—Sri Krsna; alokya—after seeing; sthitim—condition; svabhavikim—natural; api—also; darpah— pride; kandarpa—of Cupid; hrdaye—in the heart; manah—pique; manavati—of the ladies in mana; hrdi—in the heart.

**Перевод:**

**Upon seeing Sri Krsna, the pride in Cupid’s heart relinquished its natural condition, and so did the mana in the hearts of the huffy girls.**

*atra kandarpo nirdarpaḥ, mānavatyo ’pi māna-rahitā iti yadyapi vastu śabdenaiva pratīyate, tathāpi na vācaka-mukhena, na ca vācya-mukhena. vācaka-mukhena ced abhaviṣyat tadā tasyānyārtho ’bhaviṣyat. atra vācakā eva śabdāḥ, na tūktārthavyañjakāḥ. evaṁ vācya-mukhena ced abhaviṣyat tadā anyo ’py artho ’bhaviṣyat. ayaṁ tu vācya evārthaḥ, na tu vyaṅgyaḥ, tarhi sa-bādham idam ity api na vaktavyam. tathā hi, gavi śukle calati dṛṣṭe gauḥ śuklaś cala iti tritaya-vikalpo yad eva dṛṣṭaṁ tad eva vikalpayati. tac cābhinnāsaṁsṛṣṭatvena darśanaṁ bhedasaṁsargābhyāṁ vikalpayati.*

**Перевод:**

**In this verse, even though the ideas that Cupid became prideless and that the girls in mana became free of mana are understood simply through the words, they are not understood through the words’ being literally expressive nor by the literal meanings expressed by the words. If the ideas were understood through the words’ being literally expressive, it would have to be said that the ideas are additional meanings of those words. In this verse, however, all the words directly express their literal meaning; they do not suggest the meanings described in the sentence (becoming prideless and becoming free of mana). Similarly, if the ideas were understood through the literal meanings expressed by the words, it would have to be said that the ideas are additional meanings of those words.**

**The meanings described in the sentences are only literal: they are not implied. Therefore it should not be said that in paryayokta the ideas do not make sense (so that one would have to resort to figurative usage to make sense of the ideas that both pride and anger are conscious beings which have the ability to relinquish their natures). For example, in the sentence: gavi sukle calati drste gauh suklas calah, “When a white cow is seen to be moving, there is cowness, whiteness, and movement,”” the distinction of three elements (jati (the category: cowness), guna (the quality: whiteness), and kriya (the action: moving) which are apprehended in this order) makes the perception of what is seen. And those three elements, seen in the beginning to be non-differentiated and hence uncombined, are later distinguished as different and as requiring the combination.**

**Комментарий:**

At first when a white cow is seen to be moving, no distinction is perceived between cowness and the individual cow, between whiteness and the particular whiteness of the cow, or between the activity of moving in general and the particular activity of moving done by the cow at that time. Later, however one differentiates them by one’s knowledge of Nyaya and perceives how they are working together in combination.

The scheme of the paryayokta ornament is based on Mammata’s tatparya (the Purport): The meaning of the sentence is arrived at by rewording the sentence, without using Indication or Suggestiveness. Thus, Kavi Kamapura’s example ofparyayokta is a form of poetic expression classed in that way.

**♦   sad-yoga (combination of good things),**

**♦   asad-yoga (combination of bad things), and**

**♦   ubhaya-yoga (combination of good things and bad things).**

**38.   Anumāna**

### 8.224

*sādhya-sādhana-sadbhāve ’numānam anumāna-vat (50)*

**Пословный перевод:**

sadhya-sadhana—of a sadhya (what is to be proved) and of a sadhana (a cause, i.e. the proof); sad-bhave—where there is the occurrence; anumanam—the ornament called anumana; anumana- vat—like an inference.

**Перевод:**

**When a sadhya and a sadhana are expressed, that is anumana (inference). It is like an inference.**

*anumāne yathā tri-vidho hetus tathātrāpi.*

**Перевод:**

**Just as there is a threefold hetu (cause) with regard to the anumana of the Nyaya school, so the threefold hetu is present in the anumana of poetics.**

**Комментарий:**

Mammata mentions the threefold hetu, and Govinda Thakkura gives the details, but Visvanatha Kaviraja does not bother reiterating them. In usage, the anumana of poetics is a threefold process:

1\. paksa (the thing under discussion),

2\. sadhya (what is to be proved), and

3\. hetu (the proof) (also called sadhana).

The main difference between anumana and kavya-linga is that in anumana the reason is a universal rule. In addition, usually in anumana the word “therefore” or “because” is used, whereas in kavya-linga the poetical theorists do not use those words and avoid using a third case-ending or a fifth case-ending in the sense of hetu (“because”).

*atra bhavad-akṣi pakṣaḥ, manobhavasya bāṇa iti sādhyam, mānasa-bhedakatvād iti hetuḥ.*

**Перевод:**

*etad valagna-gaganāñcala-cumbi-cāru-*  
*gandhollasat-tanu-ruhāvali-dhūma-hetoḥ*

**Пословный перевод:**

nabhi— genitals (“central point”); grham— \[is\] the house; tava— your; kalavati—O expert girl; manmathasya—of Cupid; lila—in the form of \[amorous\] pastimes; agnihotra—for the Agnihotra sacrifice; bhuja—of the arms; darpa—in the form of the pride; krsanu—the fire; sali— \[the house\] possesses; etat—this; valagna— in the form of the waist; gagana—of the sky; ancala—the edge; cumbi—which are kissing; caru—nice; gandha—on account of fragrance; ullasat—resplendent; tanu-ruha—of hairs; avali—in the form of a row; dhuma-hetoh—because of a reason, which is smoke.

**Перевод:**

**Girl expert in love, your central part is Cupid’s home burning in the fire of the Agnihotra sacrifice of love, a fire which is the pride of Krsna’s arms, because arising from this sacrifice is the fragrant smoke, the row of your resplendent belly-hairs, which rises from there and kisses the sky of your waist.**

*atra rūpaka-garbham anumānam.*

**Перевод:**

**The anumana in this verse contains metaphors.**

**Комментарий:**

Visvanatha Cakravarti: “The metaphors are: (1) Her central hollow is Cupid’s home: this clause is the paksa, (2) The amorous fun is the Agnihotra sacrifice, (3) The pride of Sri Krsna’s arms is the fire of this Agnihotra sacrifice of love: this clause is the sadhya, (4) The row of hairs on her belly is the smoke, and is resplendent due to the fragrance; the clause “the row of hairs is the smoke” is the hetu, meaning it is the cause that proves the existence of the fire that is the pride of Sri Krsna’s arms, and (5) Her waist is the sky, because it is very thin.

“The overall analogy is this: Just as Brahmana priests infer, due to the presence of particularly fragrant smoke rising from a house and shooting up into the sky, the presence of the fire of an Agnihotra sacrifice, so the sakhls infer, due to the presence of the smoke that is fragrant belly hairs occurring in the sky that is her waist and rising from the house that is her central part, the occurrence of fire that is the pride of Krsna’s arms. This fire relates to the Agnihotra sacrifice which is erotic enjoyment.”

**41.   Parisaṅkhyā**

### 8.232

*praśna-pūrvakam ākhyānaṁ tat-sāmānya-vyapohanam*  
*tasya tasyāpi ca jñeye vyaṅgyatve syād athāparam*  
*apraśna-pūrvakaṁ vācyaṁ parisaṅkhyā catur-vidhā (53)*

*tasya tasya ceti praśna-pūrvākhyānasya tat-sāmānya-*  
*vyapohanasya ca vyaṅgyatvam. apraśna-pūrvakasya tat-*  
*sāmānya-vyapohanasya ca vācyatvaṁ ceti caturdhā.*

**Пословный перевод:**

prasna—by a question; purvakam—preceded; akhyanam— statement; tat—to that \[statement\]; samanya—of things that are similar; vyapohanam—the negation; tasya—of that (i.e. of a statement preceded by question); tasya—of that (i.e. of a rejection of things similar to what is stated); api—also; ca—and; jneye— is understood; vyangyatve—when the quality of being implied; syat—is; atha—then; aparam—another; aprasna-purvakam—not preceded by a question; vacyam—expressed; parisankhya—the ornament called parisankhya; caturvidha—fourfold.

**Перевод:**

**Parisankhya (answer with an exclusion) has four varieties:**

**1. prasna-purvaka-akhyanam (questions and answers),**

**2. tat-samanya-vyapohanam (rejection of things similar to what is stated),**

**3. prasna-purvakakhyanasya tat-samanya-vyapohanasya ca vyangyatvam (both the question and the rejection of things similar to what is stated are implied),**

**4. aprasna-purvakasya tat-samanya-vyapohanasya ca vacyatvam prasna-purvakatvasya vyangyatvam ca (the question is implied but the rejection of things similar to what is stated is expressed).**

**Комментарий:**

Essentially, parisankhya is an intricate uttara ornament (answer) (8.241). The difference is that in parisankhya there is a rejection.

The reason the figure is called parisankhya is this: The prefix pari is used in the sense of exclusion, by Panini’s sutra: apa-pari varjane, “Apa and pari are used in the sense of exclusion” (Astadhyayi 1.4.88). The definition of sankhya is: carca sankhya vicarana, “The words carca, sankhya, and vicarana \[are synonymous and mean discussion, deliberation\]” (Amara-kosa 1.5.2). Therefore the sense of parisankhya is: “the mention of one thing with the idea of excluding another.” For example, if the question is: “What should be sung?”, the answer, “The amorous pastimes in Vraja”, implies the negation of singing about mundane things.

*nīvi-keśa-rasanādiṣu bandhaḥ*  
*sāndra-candana-rasādiṣu paṅkaḥ*

**Пословный перевод:**

vakrata—crookedness; mrga-drsam—of the doe-eyed girls; kaca- pase—in the tresses (“in the ropes of hair”); pani-pada-nayana- adisu—in the hands, feet, eyes, and so on; ragah—redness, or material attachment; mvi-kesa-rasana-adisu—in regard to petticoats, hair bands, girdles, and so on; bandhah—bondage; sandra-candana-rasa-adisu—in reference to thick sandalwood paste and other ointments; pankah—dirt, mud.

**Перевод:**

**In Vraja, vakrata exists only in the doe-eyed girls’ tresses, raga exists only in their eyes, feet, and hands, bandha is only used in reference to their petticoats, hair bands, girdles, and so on, and panka is only used to denote their ointments such as thick sandalwood paste.**

*atra kva vakratety-ādi-praśna-pūrvakasyākhyānasya tat-sāmānyavyapohanasya ca vyaṅgyatā, tathā hi kva vakratā, mṛga-dṛśāṁ gopīnāṁ kaca-pāśa eva, nāntaḥ-karaṇādau kasyāpīty-ādi.*

**Перевод:**

**Here both the question and the rejection of things similar to what is stated are implied. For instance, the full idea is: “Where is crookedness (vakrata)?” “It is to be found only in the tresses of the doe-eyed gopis. It is not to be found in the mind of any resident of Vraja,” and so forth.**

**Комментарий:**

The implied questions are:

◊ Where is vakrata (crookedness)?

◊ Where is raga (material attachment)?

◊ Where is bandha (bondage)?

◊ Where is panka (mud)?

A nivi-bandha is a petticoat but it also refers to the ends of that cloth tied into a knot in front of the body.

A kesa-bandha is a hair band, and a rasana-bandha is a knot made with the ends of a girdle. A similar verse is text 3.19.

Kunkuma-panka and candana-panka are types of ointments.

In like manner, in Radha-kund nowadays the term vaisnava-seva is only used in the sense of food distribution.

**48.   Samādhi**

### 8.252

*kāraṇāntara-sāhāyyāt kāryaṁ yat su-karaṁ bhavet*  
*kartur vinā prayatnena sa samādhir itīryate (59)*

**Пословный перевод:**

karana—cause; antara—of different; sahayyat—because of the assistance; karyam—effect; yat—which; su-karam—in such a way that it is easily done; bhavet—is; kartuh—of the karta; vina prayatnena—without the effort; sah—that; samadhih—the ornament called samadhi; iti—thus; iryate—announced.

**Перевод:**

**Комментарий:**

P.V. Kane explains: “The name samadhi given to the figure is significant. Samadhi is equivalent to samyag adhih (adhanam karanam) ‘accomplishing a thing well.’” In that sense, the word samadhi is a synonym of angikara (acceptance) (Amara-kosa 1.5.5).

The difference between samadhi and samuccaya is this: In samuccaya, there are many causes operating to produce the same one effect, whereas in samadhi, the occurrence of another cause by chance facilitates the manifestation of the desired effect. Visvanatha Kaviraja uses the word daivat (by chance) in his definition of samadhi (Sahitya-darpana 10.85).

**When the combination of two attributes is hard to achieve due to a very great contrast between them and when the person trying to bring about that difficult-to-achieve combination fails to produce the desired result, but instead produces an undesired result, that is called visama (incongruity, disparity). There are four categories:**

**1.   A quality is contrasted by a quality,**

**2.   An action is contrasted by an action,**

**3.   A quality that is a cause is contrasted by a quality that is an effect,**

**4.   An action that is a cause is contrasted by an action that is an effect.**

**57.  Pratīpa**

### 8.277

*upamānasya dhik-kāra upameya-stutau yadi*  
*pratīpam upamānasya dhik-kṛtyai copameyatā (68)*

**Пословный перевод:**

upamanasya—the upamana; dhik-karah—making contemptible; upameya-stutau—in regard to praising the upameya; yadi— if; pratipam—the ornament called pratipa; upamanasya—the upamana; dhik-krtyai—for the sake of making contemptible; ca— and; upameyata—being the upameya.

**Перевод:**

**Praffpa (reverse simile) has two varieties: (1) The description makes the upamana (standard of comparison) look contemptible for the sake of praising the upameya, and (2) Being the upameya is only for the sake of making the upamana look contemptible.**

*upameya-stuty-artham upamāna-dhik-kāro yadi tadā pratīpaṁ, yadi vā dhik-kārāyaiva upamānasyaivopameyatā tadā ceti dvividham.*

**(The translation of this was incorporated above.)**

**Комментарий:**

The word pratlpa is formed with the prefix prati and the word ap (water), in accordance with Astadhyayi 6.3.97, which ordains the change of the a of ap to l when ap is connected to a prefix. Next, Ip becomes Ipa through the application of the suffix \[d\]a\[c\] (Astadhyayl 5.4.74). In the word pratlpa, the prefix prati is used in its sense ofpratividhi (opposition) (Visva-kosa 2.25). The sense of pratlpa is: “going against the current,” meaning “going against the grain.” The name pratlpa is given to this ornament because it consists of a reversal of a usual comparison.

### 8.279

**Перевод:**

**\[Being the upameya is only for the sake of making the upamana look contemptible:\]**

*vara-tanu nanu kṛṣṇo hanta vaidagdhya-mugdhaḥ*  
*śiva śiva bhuvi bhadrābhadra-bhāve ’nabhijñaḥ*  
*tava vigata-kalaṅkenānanenaiva yo ’yaṁ*  
*śaśinam upamimīte naiva lajjāṁ karoti*

**Пословный перевод:**

vara-tanu—O girl whose body is the best; nanu—only; krsnah— Krsna; hanta—alas; vaidagdhya - mugdhah—devoid of expertise; siva siva—alas; bhuvi—on earth; bhadra—good; abhadra—bad; bhave—in regard to the existence of; anabhijnah—not knowing; tava—Your; vigata—has gone; kalankena—from which a mark; ananena—with the face; eva—only; yah ayam—this famous one who; sasinam—the moon; upamimlte—compares; na—not; eva— certainly; lajjam karoti—is not ashamed.

Krsna turned Radha’s face into the upamana, and the moon into the upameya. However, it is a universal rule that the moon is the upamana of a face. Therefore, making the moon into an upameya is done for the purpose of belittling the moon, since by convention an upamana is superior to an upameya.

### 8.280

**Перевод:**

**\[This verse illustrates a sub-category of pratipa: \]**

*mama vadanam eva nayanā-*  
*nandakam iti mā kṛthāḥ su-tanu garvam*  
*aparo ’pi kaścid evaṁ*  
*rākāyāṁ śaradi śītāṁśuḥ*

**Пословный перевод:**

mama—my; vadanam—face; eva—only; nayana—the eyes; anandakam—delights; iti—thus; ma krthah—don’t do; su-tanu—O girl with a beautiful body; garvam—pride; aparah—another; api—also; kascit—someone (or something); evam—in this way; rakayam—in the full moon; saradi—of autumn; sita-amsuh—the moon (“whose rays are cool”).

**Комментарий:**

This is a form of pratipa because the purport is that the moon is no longer a worthy standard of comparison, since here both her face and the moon are treated as equal.

In addition, if “the moon” represents Krsna’s face, that wording constitutes the first variety of the atisayokti ornament (introsusception).

**Пословный перевод:**

prastutasya—of the subject under discussion; aprastutena— with something that is not the subject under discussion; guna— of qualities; ekatva—oneness; vivaksaya—on account of the desire to express; aikyam—oneness; nibadhyate—is constructed (described); yogat—on account of the connection; yat—where (yatra); samanyam—the ornament called samanya (“oneness”); tat—there (tatra); isyate—is defined.

The reason the ornament is called samanya is that there is a connection between two things which have the same quality, which renders them undistinguishable. *śabdaḥ śabdālaṅkāraḥ, artho ’rthālaṅkāraḥ, ubhayaṁ śabdārthālaṅkāraḥ, ete trayaḥ kriyā-pradhānā ity arthaḥ. eteṣām anyonya-nirapekṣatvena viśakalitatayāvasthānaṁ saṁsṛṣṭiḥ. tatra śabdālaṅkāra-saṁsṛṣṭir yathā—sura-tarur ity-ādau yamakānuprāsayoḥ saṁsṛṣṭiḥ.*
